topic.title: Dynamic strings and the string heap

body.p: A dynamic string, declared with VAR STRING and no capacity, is a handle to storage in a compiler-managed heap. Its contents may grow, shrink, and be concatenated at run time. Dynamic strings are supported on every target, but they need a heap whose size is fixed at compile time.

The heap size is declared with a WORD constant named _string_heap_size. It must appear before the first dynamic string and before the strings_dynamic library is included, because that library declares wrappers with STRING formals:
body.codeblock:
CONST WORD _string_heap_size = 255 INCLUDE strings_dynamic
VAR STRING name = "JALv3" VAR STRING out
body.p: Each handle holds three index-sized fields (offset, length, and capacity) plus the payload bytes, which live in the heap. The width of the index fields is selected with a pragma (see below).

section.title: Heap configuration
section.codeblock: PRAGMA STRING INDEX AUTO | BYTE | WORD PRAGMA STRING ALLOC FIRST_FIT | BEST_FIT PRAGMA STRING RETRY ON | OFF
section.p: INDEX selects the width of the per-handle offset, length, and capacity fields and of the heap block headers. AUTO chooses a width from the declared heap size; BYTE and WORD force the width.
ALLOC selects the free-block search: FIRST_FIT takes the first block that is large enough, BEST_FIT the smallest such block.
RETRY controls what happens when an allocation fails. With ON, the allocator compacts the heap once and retries the search; with OFF it fails immediately and sets the error byte.
The older PRAGMA STRING HEAP <bytes> line is still accepted, but it is ignored: it neither sets the heap size nor produces a warning. Use the _string_heap_size constant instead.

section.title: Assignment, copying, and concatenation
section.p: Assigning a literal allocates or resizes the payload. Assigning one dynamic string to another copies its contents. The & operator concatenates string values on the right-hand side of an assignment:
section.codeblock:
VAR STRING msg VAR STRING dst VAR STRING src = "world"
msg = "hello" dst = src msg = "Hello, " & src & "!" msg = msg & "" -- empty by concatenation; frees the payload
section.p: Concatenation also works in expression position: as either operand of == or !=, and as a procedure argument. The chain is evaluated into a compiler-generated heap cell and then behaves like any other dynamic string.
section.codeblock: IF msg == "Hello, " & src & "!" THEN ... END IF IF "Hi, " & src == msg THEN ... END IF print_string(serial_data, "t=" & src)
section.p: The & operator remains the bitwise AND when the left operand is not a string, so conditions such as (c1 == 1) & (c2 == 2) keep their meaning. Once a string operand has been seen, a non-string operand after & is a compile error.

section.title: Numbers in concatenations
section.p: Integer operands, constants and variables alike, render as ASCII decimal inside a & chain. All integer widths are supported, signed and unsigned, with a leading minus for negative values. Hexadecimal literals render in decimal too: 0x10 becomes "16".
section.codeblock:
VAR BYTE cnt = 42 VAR DWORD addr = 4294967295 VAR SQWORD big = -1234567890
out = "cnt=" & cnt & " addr=" & addr out = "neg: " & -42 & " sqw: " & big
section.p: Floating point constants render as shortest round-trip decimal, so 1.5 becomes "1.5", 100.0 becomes "100", and 1e-8 becomes "0.00000001". Runtime floating point variables and BIT values are not converted and produce a clean compile error.

section.title: Length and errors
section.p: COUNT returns the current character count of a dynamic string, which is not the same as the capacity of a fixed-capacity string. The _length(expr) spelling is still accepted; with -warn-misc the compiler suggests COUNT instead.

The shared byte _string_error records the result of the most recent string operation. Reading it returns the stored code and resets the byte to none, so read it once per operation when the exact code matters. The symbolic constants are string_error_none, string_error_heap_full, string_error_overflow, and string_error_invalid.
section.codeblock: VAR BYTE err = _string_error IF err == string_error_heap_full THEN ... END IF
section.p: An assignment that fails for lack of heap space leaves the destination string unchanged and records string_error_heap_full.

section.title: Library helpers
section.p: After INCLUDE strings_dynamic the following functions are available. They return a BIT: TRUE on success, FALSE on failure or truncation.
section.codeblock: string_append(string IN OUT dst, STRING IN src) string_append_truncate(string IN OUT dst, STRING IN src, WORD IN max_len) string_truncate(STRING IN OUT dst, WORD IN max_len) string_from_array(STRING IN OUT dst, BYTE IN src_array[]) string_from_array_truncate(STRING IN OUT dst, BYTE IN src_array[], WORD IN max_len) string_to_array(BYTE OUT dst_array[], STRING IN src) string_to_array_truncate(BYTE OUT dst_array[], STRING IN src, WORD IN max_len) string_heap_compact()
section.p: The truncating helpers return FALSE when bytes were dropped. The same built-ins may also be spelled with a leading underscore, for example _string_append and _string_heap_compact.
string_heap_compact() packs the live heap blocks and patches every dynamic handle's offset. It returns FALSE when the work table cannot be emitted or heap support is missing.

section.title: Pointers to dynamic strings
section.p: A pointer whose pointee contract is VAR STRING can be bound to a dynamic string, and assignments and concatenations through the pointer operate on the string it refers to. See .
section.codeblock: VAR POINTER p AS VAR STRING p IS name p = "hello" p = p & " tail"
